records.our_prose: The tomatillo (Physalis philadelphica) is a warm-season Solanaceae grown for its tart, husk-covered fruit, the green base of salsa verde. Culture mirrors tomato, started indoors and transplanted after frost, with three differences worth knowing. First, it is self-incompatible: a single plant sets almost no fruit, so grow at least two for cross-pollination. Second, the plant is large, sprawling, and vigorous, reaching 3 to 4 feet tall and wide, so it needs a sturdy cage or stake and wide spacing. Third, it tolerates summer heat and drought better than tomato and is notably less disease-prone, which makes it forgiving across hot regions. Fruit is ready when it swells to fill, and often split, its papery husk. Plants are heavy bearers and self-seed readily from dropped fruit, so expect volunteers the following spring.

records.our_prose: Tomatillo plants can run into a few common problems. Blight is a leaf disease that shows up first on the bottom leaves and spreads fastest in wet, humid weather. Blossom end rot is the black or brown sunken spot on the bottom of the tomatillo, it looks like a nutrient problem, but it's almost always caused by uneven watering (dry one day, soaked the next). Adding calcium won't fix it. Steady moisture will.
